text.p: Aluminium prices hit two-year lows overnight in London on investment fund sales and rising inventories.
Copper prices dropped in tandem and nickel prices softened.
Gold prices edged lower, but after the close of New York trade U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the IMF was very close to an agreement to sell off some of its gold.
Oil prices surged on news Iraq had attacked a U.S. fighter over Iraq and on the consequent talk of retaliation by U.S. officials.
Wheat prices also surged on a higher USDA forecast of world wheat production. The USDA lifted Australia's forecast by two million tonnes to 19.5 million tonnes.
The CRB Index closed down 0.92 of a point at 247.22.

Base metal prices gravitated towards the lower reaches of Wednesday's trading ranges during afternoon LME trading, as a depressed aluminium market pointed the way lower for the rest of the complex, traders said.

Copper closed the kerb at $1,915, down $9 from yesterday. The cash/threes spread was at a $12/16 backwardation. Nickel prices remained softer during the afternoon rings and kerb, staging a downward reaction to early 2-1/2 month highs when prices were lifted by news of a furnace explosion at PT Inco in Indonesia.

COMEX copper futures fell sharply to end at seven week lows Wednesday, led down by LME copper which also fell to seven week lows. COMEX December fell 2.85 cents to 87.15 a lb after hitting a session low at 87.00, its lowest level since July 22.
Aluminium hit a two year low of $1,437 a tonne and closed just above this level, with the market knocked by investment fund sales after expected consumer interest failed to emerge.

Inventories are increasing and consumers show little sign of buying anything more than hand-to-mouth requirements, which prompted stale bull liquidation today and suggests further losses are inevitable.
Other metals saw early uptrends interrupted and then negated by aluminium's weakness, with copper similarly heading for a test of key levels on the downside, traders said.

New York precious metals futures ended slightly lower Wednesday, after the U.S. Federal Reserve's beige book found evidence of inflation inconclusive and despite some nervousness about further hostilities in Iraq which helped to firm prices early in the session.
COMEX December gold ended off 20 cents at $386.60 an ounce, after firming early to an session high at $387.70, helped by nervousness about more hostilities in Iraq.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold closed quoted $383.00/383.50, compared to the London afternoon fix at $383.50, and a New York close Tuesday at $383.00-383.40.

After the market closed, U.S. Treasury Secretary Rubin said IMF members were "very close to an agreement" on selling some gold reserves to help finance the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) which is designed to alleviate the debt of developing countries.

All three legs of the NYMEX oil complex ended higher after reaching life-of-contract highs in the spot month in a rally sparked by news Iraq fired missiles at U.S. jets in northern Iraq, traders said.

"The market is worried that the tension in Iraq could escalate even more every time the U.S. flies over the no-fly zone," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products at Paribas Futures Inc. U.S. jets were patrolling a "no-fly" zone set by the United States and allied forces after the 1991 Gulf War.
October crude settled up 63 cents at $24.75 a barrel. October crude reached a life-of-contract high Wednesday of $24.98.
The post-Gulf War high for crude is $25.70.
"This just delays the oil-for-food deal further but it's broader than that. There is a conflict in an oil rich region," said a trader of the tensions in Iraq.
CBOT wheat futures closed lower on confirmation Wednesday by USDA that U.S. and world supplies of wheat were increasing, traders said.
USDA early Wednesday tabbed 1996 U.S. wheat production at 2.296 billion bushels, above the average of analysts' expectations for 2.268 billion.

The government also boosted its estimate for world wheat ending stocks to 117.43 million tonnes, up 8.75 million from its outlook in August for 108.68 million. USDA further increased its outlook for Australian wheat production this year to 19.5 million tonnes, up two million from its August forecast.
Wheat closed 11 to 17-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with September down 17-1/2 at $4.44 a bushel.

CSCE world sugar futures headed lower Wednesday, led by broad losses on the spot October contract. Selling by commission houses kept the market under pressure through most of the session, after an early round of trade buying failed to gather steam.
March, May July and October 1997 futures briefly hit fresh life-of-contract highs before retreating.
Speculators continued to roll long postions into March ahead of the October contract's expiry at the end of the month.
October fell 0.09 cent a lb on the day, to 11.96, ranging from 11.94 to 12.12. March eased 0.07 to 1.66, while the remaining months finished even to down 0.04.
